title: Voice AI, On-Device vs Cloud & Moderation Architecture
scopeHtml: Scope: Streaming voice with interruptions and turn-taking, on-device vs cloud trade-offs, moderation thresholds and human review.

notes.title: Where the model runs: device or cloud
notes.html:
An AI model is just a big file of numbers (weights) plus code that multiplies them. "On-device" means that file lives on the phone and the phone's CPU, GPU or NPU (neural processing unit, a chip built for matrix math) runs it. "Cloud" means you send the input over the network to a server with big GPUs, and get the answer back. Everything in this note is a consequence of that single choice.

Why both exist: a phone has maybe 6 to 12 GB of RAM shared with every other app, a battery, and a chip that throttles when hot. A data center GPU has tens of GB of fast memory and wall power. So the cloud can run a model that is 100 times bigger and smarter. But the cloud is far away, costs money per request, and sees your data. The device is right there, free per request, and private, but small.

Typical split in real products:

Task Usual home Why
Keyboard next-word suggestion On-device Must answer in under 50 ms, works offline
Wake word ("Hey Google") On-device Always listening; sending audio to the cloud would be a privacy and battery disaster
Smart reply, summarise short text On-device (Gemini Nano via AICore / ML Kit GenAI, verify availability per device) Small task, private
Long research answer, coding, complex reasoning Cloud Needs a frontier model
Photo OCR, face detection On-device Tiny models, mature
Moderation of user uploads Cloud (server side) You must not trust the client to police itself

The last row is the first interview trap: anything that is a safety or business control must run on a machine you own, never only on the device the user controls, because the user can modify the app.

            +-------------------+
 user ----> |  App on phone     |
            |  small model      |--- easy / private / offline --> answer
            +---------+---------+
                      | hard / long / needs fresh data
                      v
            +-------------------+
            |  Your backend     |
            |  big model, tools |--> answer
            +-------------------+

Analogy (after the explanation): on-device is the pocket calculator in your bag, instant and private but only does arithmetic. Cloud is phoning a professor: far smarter, but you wait for them to pick up, you pay, and you tell them your problem.

See also in other C8 notes: reference architecture and latency budgets (01_A1, 03_D1).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "on-device is always faster". A small model on a weak phone can generate 5 to 15 tokens per second; a cloud model may stream faster after a network round trip. Faster to first byte is not faster to finish.
  • Putting API keys or moderation logic only in the app. The app is untrusted code.
  • Forgetting that on-device models differ per phone. Capability depends on RAM, chip and OS version, so you need a feature check and fallback.

notes.title: Comparing latency, privacy and battery
notes.html:
Take each axis and put numbers on it. All numbers below are illustrative orders of magnitude, not benchmarks; measure on your own devices (verify).

Latency has two parts. Time to first token (TTFT) is the wait before anything appears. Throughput is tokens per second afterwards.

Cloud request, text answer of 200 tokens
  network round trip (mobile)      80 - 200 ms   (radio wake-up can add more)
  server queue + prefill           200 - 800 ms
  decode at ~50 tok/s              200 / 50 = 4.0 s total streaming
  user sees first token at         ~0.3 - 1.0 s, full answer ~4.5 s

On-device 3B-class model, 200 tokens
  load model into memory (cold)    1 - 5 s  (zero if kept warm)
  prefill short prompt              100 - 500 ms
  decode at ~10 tok/s              200 / 10 = 20 s total
  user sees first token at         ~0.2 - 0.6 s warm, full answer ~20 s

So on-device wins TTFT when warm and on short outputs, and loses on long outputs. That is why on-device suits short, structured tasks.

Privacy: with cloud, data leaves the device. Your obligations grow: encryption in transit, retention policy, a data processing agreement with the model vendor, regional rules (GDPR, HIPAA, India DPDP, verify what applies), and a bigger breach surface. On-device means the text never leaves, which can remove whole classes of compliance work. But note "private" is not "safe": a model on the device can still be jailbroken by its owner, and you get no server logs to investigate abuse.

Battery: radio is expensive. Waking the cellular modem and holding it high-power costs energy per burst, and long streaming keeps it awake. Local inference costs energy through sustained compute, and a phone running an LLM flat out for 20 seconds can warm up and throttle (the OS lowers clock speed, so tokens per second drops mid-answer). Rule of thumb: many tiny requests are bad on the cloud (radio tail), long generations are bad on-device (heat). Battery drain per task is hard to guess; use Android Battery Historian or Perfetto, and the energy profiler, rather than trusting a formula.

Cost is the fourth axis people forget: on-device inference costs you nothing per call, cloud costs per token. A feature used 50 times a day by 10 million users makes that free-per-call property worth real money.

Analogy: the short walk to the corner shop (on-device) beats a car trip for a bottle of milk, but loses to the car for a week's groceries.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting one latency number. Always separate TTFT from total time and say warm vs cold.
  • Claiming on-device saves battery by default. It trades radio energy for compute energy and heat.
  • Ignoring model download size. A 1 to 3 GB model must be downloaded once, on Wi-Fi, with a progress and a fallback while it arrives.
  • Treating privacy as binary. Say what leaves the device, who can read it and how long it is kept.

notes.title: A hybrid router with fallback
notes.html:
Real apps rarely choose one side. They route per request: try local when the task is simple, input is sensitive, or the network is bad; go to the cloud otherwise; and fall back the other way on failure. The router is a few dozen lines and the interesting part is the policy.

Policy inputs: is the on-device model available and warm, is the network good, is the data marked sensitive, how long is the expected output, and does the user's setting allow cloud.

request
  |
  +-- sensitive and local available? --yes--> LOCAL
  |
  +-- offline? --------------------- yes--> LOCAL (or "unavailable" message)
  |
  +-- short task (<= ~300 tokens in/out)? yes--> LOCAL, on error -> CLOUD
  |
  +-- otherwise ------------------------------> CLOUD, on timeout -> LOCAL (degraded)
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Req:
    text: str
    sensitive: bool = False
    expected_tokens: int = 100

def route(req, local_ok: bool, online: bool, cloud_allowed: bool) -> str:
    if req.sensitive and local_ok:
        return "local"
    if not online or not cloud_allowed:
        return "local" if local_ok else "unavailable"
    if local_ok and req.expected_tokens <= 300:
        return "local"
    return "cloud"

# prints: local
print(route(Req("summarise this note", expected_tokens=80), True, True, True))
data class Req(val text: String, val sensitive: Boolean = false, val expectedTokens: Int = 100)

fun route(req: Req, localOk: Boolean, online: Boolean, cloudAllowed: Boolean): String = when {
    req.sensitive && localOk -> "local"
    !online || !cloudAllowed -> if (localOk) "local" else "unavailable"
    localOk && req.expectedTokens <= 300 -> "local"
    else -> "cloud"
}

fun main() {
    // prints: local
    println(route(Req("summarise this note", expectedTokens = 80), true, true, true))
}
public class Router {
    record Req(String text, boolean sensitive, int expectedTokens) {}

    static String route(Req req, boolean localOk, boolean online, boolean cloudAllowed) {
        if (req.sensitive() && localOk) return "local";
        if (!online || !cloudAllowed) return localOk ? "local" : "unavailable";
        if (localOk && req.expectedTokens() <= 300) return "local";
        return "cloud";
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // prints: local
        System.out.println(route(new Req("summarise this note", false, 80), true, true, true));
    }
}

On Android the localOk flag comes from asking the platform whether the on-device model is downloaded and usable (ML Kit GenAI / AICore status checks, or whether your MediaPipe LLM Inference model file exists; exact method names vary, verify in the docs). Never call the cloud model directly from the app with a key; call your own proxy, which holds ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in an environment variable.

Real examples: Google's Gemini Nano runs on supported Pixel and Samsung phones for features like summaries and smart replies while heavier Gemini requests go to the cloud; Apple Intelligence runs a small local model and escalates to its Private Cloud Compute for larger requests (verify current details); Whisper-class speech recognition is often run locally for dictation.

Production failure patterns: the router says "local" but the model was evicted from memory, so the first call takes 4 seconds; the local model outputs garbage on a low-RAM phone and nobody notices because there are no server logs; the cloud fallback silently doubles your bill during an on-device outage. Log which path served each request, and alert on the ratio.

Analogy: a call-centre triage desk. Easy questions are answered by the front desk, hard ones are passed to a specialist, and if the specialist is out the desk gives the best answer it can.

Common interview traps.

  • Routing by guesswork with no logging. You cannot tune a router you cannot observe.
  • Falling back from cloud to local without telling the user the answer may be weaker.
  • Forgetting a consent flag: some users disallow cloud processing entirely.

notes.title: Voice AI: the pipeline from microphone to speaker
notes.html:
A voice assistant listens, understands, thinks and speaks. Define the pieces: ASR (automatic speech recognition, also STT, speech to text) turns audio into words. The LLM decides what to say. TTS (text to speech) turns words into audio. VAD (voice activity detection) decides whether someone is currently speaking.

There are two architectures.

Cascade: mic -> VAD -> ASR -> LLM -> TTS -> speaker. Each stage is a separate model, you can swap them, inspect the text in the middle (great for moderation and logging), and mix on-device and cloud. Cost: delays add up.

Speech-to-speech (native audio models, such as OpenAI's Realtime API or Gemini Live; verify current names): one model takes audio in and gives audio out. Lower latency, preserves tone and emotion, handles interruptions natively. Cost: less control, harder to inspect, and moderation must work on audio or on a side transcript.

CASCADE
 mic --> [VAD] --> [ASR streaming] --> [LLM streaming] --> [TTS streaming] --> speaker
          |            |partial text       |token stream        |audio chunks
          +--- end-of-turn decision --------+                   +--- cancel on barge-in

SPEECH-TO-SPEECH
 mic --> [ one audio model over a WebSocket / WebRTC ] --> speaker

The golden rule of the cascade is that every stage must stream. If ASR waits for the full sentence, the LLM waits for the full transcript, and TTS waits for the full reply, latencies add: 1 s + 1.5 s + 1 s = 3.5 s of silence. If each stage hands partial output forward, the user hears the first word of the reply within roughly the sum of first-chunk times, which can be under a second.

Latency budget for one turn (illustrative, verify by measuring):

end-of-speech detection (endpointing)   300 - 700 ms
ASR final result after endpoint          50 - 200 ms
LLM time to first token                  250 - 600 ms
TTS time to first audio chunk            100 - 300 ms
network + audio buffering                 50 - 200 ms
-----------------------------------------------------
total                                    750 - 2000 ms   (target for natural feel: ~800 - 1000 ms)

Humans leave gaps of roughly 200 ms between turns in conversation, so anything past a second feels laggy. The biggest lever is usually endpointing, not the model.

Real products: Alexa, Google Assistant and Siri use on-device wake word plus cloud ASR; Whisper (open model) and Deepgram, AssemblyAI, Google Speech-to-Text offer streaming ASR; ElevenLabs, Cartesia, Google and Azure TTS offer streaming synthesis; LiveKit Agents and Pipecat are open frameworks that wire this cascade together over WebRTC (verify current APIs).

Analogy: a relay race where each runner starts running as soon as the baton is partly passed, instead of waiting for the previous runner to finish and shake hands.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing the pipeline as sequential request/response. The whole point is overlapping streaming stages.
  • Choosing speech-to-speech and then being unable to moderate or log. State the trade-off.
  • Using HTTP request/response for audio. Audio needs a persistent channel: WebSocket or WebRTC.

notes.title: Streaming audio in and out
notes.html:
Audio is sent as small frames. Common choice: 16 kHz, 16-bit, mono PCM (pulse-code modulation, raw samples) for ASR. Bytes per second = 16,000 samples x 2 bytes = 32,000 B/s, so a 20 ms frame is 640 bytes (16,000 x 0.02 = 320 samples x 2 bytes). Opus compresses this to a few kB/s for the network; telephone systems use 8 kHz.

The client keeps a WebSocket open, sends frames as they are recorded, and receives events: partial transcripts, final transcripts, LLM text, and TTS audio chunks. The client plays audio from a small jitter buffer (typically 40 to 100 ms) to smooth network variation.

client                               server
  |-- audio frame (20ms) ----------->|
  |-- audio frame ------------------>|--> ASR partial "what is the wea"
  |<-- event: partial text ----------|
  |-- audio frame ------------------>|--> endpoint detected
  |<-- event: final text ------------|--> LLM streams tokens --> TTS
  |<-- audio chunk (reply) ----------|
  |<-- audio chunk ------------------|

A minimal server loop in Python with an asyncio queue shows the shape. The ASR and TTS calls are placeholders (use your vendor's streaming SDK); the point is the concurrent structure.

import asyncio

async def mic_frames(q: asyncio.Queue):
    for i in range(5):                      # pretend 5 frames of 20 ms
        await q.put(b"\x00" * 640)          # 640 bytes = 320 samples x 2 bytes
        await asyncio.sleep(0.02)
    await q.put(None)                       # end marker

async def asr_consumer(q: asyncio.Queue):
    n = 0
    while (frame := await q.get()) is not None:
        n += len(frame)                     # here: send frame to streaming ASR
    print("received bytes:", n)             # prints: received bytes: 3200

async def main():
    q = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=50)           # bounded: backpressure instead of memory growth
    await asyncio.gather(mic_frames(q), asr_consumer(q))

asyncio.run(main())
import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val ch = Channel<ByteArray>(capacity = 50)      // bounded buffer
    val producer = launch {
        repeat(5) { ch.send(ByteArray(640)); delay(20) }  // 20 ms frames
        ch.close()
    }
    var n = 0
    for (frame in ch) n += frame.size               // here: send frame to streaming ASR
    producer.join()
    println("received bytes: $n")                   // prints: received bytes: 3200
}
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class AudioLoop {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        BlockingQueue<byte[]> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(50);   // bounded buffer
        Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
            try {
                for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { q.put(new byte[640]); Thread.sleep(20); }
                q.put(new byte[0]);                                // end marker
            } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        });
        producer.start();
        int n = 0;
        byte[] f;
        while ((f = q.take()).length > 0) n += f.length;           // here: send to streaming ASR
        System.out.println("received bytes: " + n);                // prints: received bytes: 3200
    }
}

On Android the recording side is AudioRecord (16 kHz, ENCODING_PCM_16BIT, mono) read in a loop on a background thread, and playback is AudioTrack or ExoPlayer; use a foreground service with microphone type for background capture (permission rules differ by API level, verify). Enable acoustic echo cancellation (the AcousticEchoCanceler effect or VOICE_COMMUNICATION audio source) or the assistant will hear its own voice through the speaker and respond to itself.

Production failure patterns: unbounded queues causing memory blow-up when the network stalls; sample-rate mismatch making speech sound like chipmunks; Bluetooth headsets switching codecs mid-call and adding 200 ms; WebSocket idle timeouts at load balancers killing quiet sessions (send pings).

Analogy: a water pipe, not a bucket. You never wait for the whole tank to fill; you size the pipe and handle pressure (backpressure) when downstream is slow.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting echo cancellation, which causes self-interruption loops.
  • Unbounded buffers. Say "bounded queue plus drop or slow policy".
  • Mixing up sample rates between capture, ASR and TTS.

notes.title: Turn-taking and end-of-turn detection
notes.html:
Turn-taking is deciding whose turn it is. The system must know when the user has finished (so it can reply) without cutting them off mid-thought, and without waiting so long it feels dead.

The simplest method is VAD plus a silence timer: when no speech is detected for N ms, the turn is over. VAD can be a small model (Silero VAD, WebRTC VAD) running locally in a few ms per frame. The choice of N is the whole trade-off:

N = 300 ms : snappy, but cuts people off at every thinking pause ("I want to... book a flight")
N = 700 ms : feels natural for short commands
N = 1200 ms: safe for long dictation, but every reply feels slow

Better systems add a semantic end-of-turn model: it looks at the partial transcript (and prosody, the pitch falling at the end of a statement) and decides if the sentence is complete. "Book me a flight to" is clearly unfinished, so it extends the wait; "Yes" is complete, so it replies fast. Adaptive endpointing: short timeout when the transcript is a complete sentence, long timeout when it is not. LiveKit and others ship turn-detector models for this (verify current names).

Speculative generation is another trick: start the LLM on the partial transcript at a short silence, and if the user keeps talking, discard the work. You trade extra compute for latency.

def end_of_turn(silence_ms: int, transcript: str) -> bool:
    complete = transcript.rstrip().endswith((".", "?", "!")) or len(transcript.split()) <= 2
    limit = 400 if complete else 1000       # adaptive endpointing
    return silence_ms >= limit

# prints: True False
print(end_of_turn(450, "What time is it?"), end_of_turn(450, "Book me a flight to"))
fun endOfTurn(silenceMs: Int, transcript: String): Boolean {
    val t = transcript.trimEnd()
    val complete = t.endsWith(".") || t.endsWith("?") || t.endsWith("!") || t.split(" ").size <= 2
    val limit = if (complete) 400 else 1000   // adaptive endpointing
    return silenceMs >= limit
}

fun main() {
    // prints: true false
    println("${endOfTurn(450, "What time is it?")} ${endOfTurn(450, "Book me a flight to")}")
}
public class Turn {
    static boolean endOfTurn(int silenceMs, String transcript) {
        String t = transcript.stripTrailing();
        boolean complete = t.endsWith(".") || t.endsWith("?") || t.endsWith("!")
                || t.split("\\s+").length <= 2;
        int limit = complete ? 400 : 1000;     // adaptive endpointing
        return silenceMs >= limit;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // prints: true false
        System.out.println(endOfTurn(450, "What time is it?") + " " + endOfTurn(450, "Book me a flight to"));
    }
}

The ASR transcript from a streaming model has no reliable punctuation until it finalises, so real systems rely on the ASR vendor's own endpoint signal or a dedicated model rather than string checks; the snippet above only shows the idea.

Failure patterns: background noise (TV, café) keeps VAD "speaking" so the turn never ends; a user with a speech pause or non-native speaker gets cut off repeatedly; telephony line noise triggers false starts. Mitigate with noise suppression (RNNoise or vendor-side), tunable thresholds per channel, and a push-to-talk fallback.

Analogy: a polite dinner conversation. You notice a downward tone and a complete sentence, not just a pause, before you speak.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming silence alone is enough. Pauses within a sentence are normal.
  • Not mentioning the trade-off between false cut-offs and slow replies.
  • Treating VAD as speech recognition. VAD only says speech/not speech.

notes.title: Interruptions and barge-in
notes.html:
Barge-in means the user starts talking while the assistant is still speaking. A good assistant must stop talking quickly, throw away what it was about to say, and listen. A bad one keeps talking over the user for three more seconds.

Step by step:

1. Assistant is playing TTS audio (chunks 1..8 queued, chunk 3 playing)
2. VAD (running on mic input, after echo cancellation) fires "user speech"
3. Wait a short confirmation window (~150-300 ms) so a cough or "mm-hm" is not a barge-in
4. Confirmed -> cancel LLM stream, cancel TTS stream, flush playback buffer
5. Record how much was actually PLAYED: "I said: 'Your order will arrive on Tuesday and'"
6. Truncate conversation history to what the user actually heard
7. Start a new user turn

Step 6 is the one people miss. The LLM generated the full reply, but the user only heard half. If you keep the whole reply in the history, the model believes the user already knows the unheard part and the conversation goes wrong. Track played audio duration or word timestamps from TTS and trim the assistant message to match. (OpenAI's Realtime API exposes a truncate event for this purpose; verify the current event names.)

Back-channels ("uh-huh", "right") should not interrupt. Classify short utterances under about 500 ms or a few words as non-interrupting, or require a minimum speech duration before cancelling.

A clean cancellation design uses one cancellable task per turn:

import asyncio

async def speak(chunks, played):
    for c in chunks:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)          # pretend playback of one chunk
        played.append(c)

async def main():
    played = []
    task = asyncio.create_task(speak(["Your", "order", "arrives", "Tuesday"], played))
    await asyncio.sleep(0.25)             # user barges in here
    task.cancel()                          # cancel playback (and upstream LLM/TTS in real code)
    try:
        await task
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        pass
    print("heard:", " ".join(played))      # prints: heard: Your order

asyncio.run(main())
import kotlinx.coroutines.*

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val played = mutableListOf<String>()
    val job = launch {
        for (c in listOf("Your", "order", "arrives", "Tuesday")) {
            delay(100)                      // pretend playback of one chunk
            played += c
        }
    }
    delay(250)                              // user barges in here
    job.cancelAndJoin()                     // cancels the coroutine tree (LLM/TTS too in real code)
    println("heard: ${played.joinToString(" ")}")   // prints: heard: Your order
}
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class BargeIn {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        List<String> played = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
        ExecutorService ex = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
        Future<?> f = ex.submit(() -> {
            try {
                for (String c : List.of("Your", "order", "arrives", "Tuesday")) {
                    Thread.sleep(100);              // pretend playback of one chunk
                    played.add(c);
                }
            } catch (InterruptedException ignored) {}
        });
        Thread.sleep(250);                          // user barges in here
        f.cancel(true);                             // interrupts the thread
        ex.shutdown();
        System.out.println("heard: " + String.join(" ", played));   // prints: heard: Your order
    }
}

Real products: Alexa and Google Assistant stop on "stop" and on new wake words; phone IVR systems often disable barge-in during legal disclaimers on purpose; Gemini Live and ChatGPT voice mode support natural interruption.

Failure patterns: no echo cancellation so the speaker's own voice triggers barge-in (the assistant interrupts itself in a stutter loop); cancellation that stops audio but not the LLM, so you keep paying for tokens nobody hears; stale audio chunks arriving after cancel and playing anyway (fix with a turn id on every chunk and drop mismatches); tool calls that were mid-flight (a payment) not being cancelled or reconciled.

Analogy: a person reading aloud who stops when you say "wait", and then remembers exactly which sentence they had reached.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to truncate history to what was heard.
  • Cancelling playback but not upstream generation, which wastes money.
  • Not tagging chunks with a turn id, leading to ghost audio.
  • Treating every sound as barge-in.

notes.title: Voice latency, cost and on-device pieces
notes.html:
Voice makes the on-device vs cloud question sharper because each stage can sit in either place. A sensible split:

wake word        on-device always (tiny model, always-on, battery-critical)
VAD              on-device (cheap, saves uploading silence)
ASR              on-device for short commands (Whisper-small class, or the OS recogniser)
                 cloud for long, noisy or multilingual audio
LLM              cloud for reasoning; small local model for fixed commands ("set a timer")
TTS              on-device for fast, free, offline voice (Android TextToSpeech engine)
                 cloud for high-quality neural voices

Uploading only after VAD says speech cuts bandwidth. A 10 s clip of 16 kHz 16-bit PCM is 32,000 B/s x 10 = 320 kB uncompressed; with silence removed from a call that is 60% silence, the data uploaded drops to 128 kB (320 x 0.4). Cloud ASR is typically billed per audio second, so VAD trimming also cuts cost.

Cost sketch for a cascade turn (use your own vendor prices, mark verify): ASR billed per second of audio, LLM per input and output token, TTS per character. A 5 s question (5 s ASR), 150 reply tokens and about 600 characters of TTS adds up three separate line items; speech-to-speech models bill audio tokens and are often more expensive per minute than a cascade. Always compute cost per conversation minute and compare to revenue.

Offline voice example: a car navigation app must work in a tunnel, so it ships a local ASR for a fixed command grammar ("navigate home", "mute") and uses the cloud only for free-form questions. A "degraded mode" message ("I can only do basic commands right now") is better than silence.

Failure patterns: the first-call model load delay on-device (keep it warm or show a "listening" indicator immediately); mismatched language between ASR and TTS; high-quality cloud TTS that fails and leaves the user with no audio (always have the local engine as fallback).

Analogy: a restaurant where the waiter handles simple orders at the table (on-device) and sends only the complicated special requests to the head chef (cloud).

Common interview traps.

  • Sending continuous audio to the cloud without VAD gating.
  • Forgetting a fallback voice when the cloud TTS fails.
  • Comparing only model quality, not cost per conversation minute.

notes.title: Moderation architecture: layers before and after the model
notes.html:
Moderation means checking content for harm (hate, sexual content, self-harm, violence, harassment, illegal advice, personal data leaks) and deciding what to do. It exists because models can be tricked into harmful output, users post harmful input, and platforms carry legal and reputational responsibility.

It is an architecture, not one call. Check at four points:

 user input --> [1 input filter] --> LLM / feature --> [2 output filter] --> user
                    |                     |                    |
                    v                     v                    v
              block / allow        [3 tool/action gate]   block / rewrite / allow
                    |                                          |
                    +------------> [4 async audit + human review queue] <---+
  1. Input filter: fast, cheap checks before spending model money. Rules (blocklists, regex for card numbers), then a classifier (a small model or an API such as OpenAI's moderation endpoint, Google Perspective, or Llama Guard, an open safety classifier; verify current availability) returning a score per category.
  2. Output filter: the model can produce unsafe text from a harmless prompt, so check outputs too. For streaming this is hard: you may already have shown the first words. Options: buffer a sentence before showing it, run the check on chunks and cut the stream, or accept a short delay.
  3. Action gate: for agents with tools, the dangerous thing is an action (send email, refund). Require policy checks or approval, independent of text moderation.
  4. Async audit: sample conversations after the fact, review them, find new abuse patterns, and feed labels back into the classifier.

Voice-specific points: moderate the transcript in the cascade, which is easy. In speech-to-speech you must either run a parallel ASR on the audio for a text check or use an audio-capable classifier; accept that the unsafe audio may already be playing, so keep a quick "stop playback" path. Also consider age (voice products used by children have stricter rules, verify the law in your region) and audio-only attacks like hidden commands.

A principle: the moderator is a separate component from the model that generates. Asking the same model to police itself in the same prompt is weaker than an independent classifier, because a prompt injection that fools one fools both.

Real products: OpenAI moderation endpoint, Azure AI Content Safety, Anthropic's guidance on safeguards and classifier-based approaches, Meta Llama Guard, AWS Bedrock Guardrails, Google's Perspective API (verify each product's current status and categories).

Analogy: airport security has a check at the door, another at the gate, and cameras that supervisors review later. No single check is trusted alone.

Common interview traps.

  • Moderating only the input and forgetting the model's output.
  • Using the generating model as its own judge in the same call.
  • Doing moderation client-side only.
  • Ignoring streaming: the user may read half a harmful sentence before the filter fires.

notes.title: Thresholds: turning scores into decisions
notes.html:
A classifier returns a score (probability-like number) per category, say hate: 0.82. A threshold turns that into a decision. Two thresholds, not one, give you three outcomes:

score:   0.0 ------------- 0.40 ----------------- 0.85 ------------- 1.0
         ALLOW              SEND TO HUMAN REVIEW        AUTO-BLOCK

Why two: below the low line you are confident it is fine; above the high line you are confident it is bad; in between the model is unsure, and that is exactly where human time is most valuable.

Precision and recall are the trade-off. Precision: of what I blocked, how much was truly bad. Recall: of all truly bad content, how much did I catch. Lowering a threshold raises recall and lowers precision (more false positives, angry users). Raising it does the reverse (more harm slips through). Worked example on 10,000 items where 100 are truly bad:

Threshold 0.9: blocks 60 items, 55 truly bad  -> precision 55/60  = 91.7%, recall 55/100 = 55%
Threshold 0.5: blocks 140 items, 90 truly bad -> precision 90/140 = 64.3%, recall 90/100 = 90%

(These counts are made-up numbers to show the arithmetic.) Which is right depends on harm severity: for child safety or self-harm, accept lower precision and send many items to humans; for a mild profanity filter in a gaming chat, favour precision.

Per-category thresholds are standard: self-harm gets a low threshold and a special response (show a helpline, not just a refusal), spam gets a high one. Per-surface too: a children's app has stricter lines than a developer tool. Set thresholds from labelled data of your own traffic, not from vendor defaults, and re-measure, because language, slang and attackers change.

THRESH = {"hate": (0.40, 0.85), "self_harm": (0.20, 0.70), "spam": (0.60, 0.95)}

def decide(scores: dict) -> str:
    verdict = "allow"
    for cat, s in scores.items():
        low, high = THRESH.get(cat, (0.40, 0.85))
        if s >= high:
            return "block"                # worst case wins immediately
        if s >= low:
            verdict = "review"
    return verdict

# prints: review
print(decide({"hate": 0.5, "spam": 0.1}))
val thresh = mapOf(
    "hate" to (0.40 to 0.85),
    "self_harm" to (0.20 to 0.70),
    "spam" to (0.60 to 0.95),
)

fun decide(scores: Map<String, Double>): String {
    var verdict = "allow"
    for ((cat, s) in scores) {
        val (low, high) = thresh[cat] ?: (0.40 to 0.85)
        if (s >= high) return "block"      // worst case wins immediately
        if (s >= low) verdict = "review"
    }
    return verdict
}

fun main() {
    // prints: review
    println(decide(mapOf("hate" to 0.5, "spam" to 0.1)))
}
import java.util.Map;

public class Decide {
    static final Map<String, double[]> THRESH = Map.of(
        "hate", new double[]{0.40, 0.85},
        "self_harm", new double[]{0.20, 0.70},
        "spam", new double[]{0.60, 0.95});

    static String decide(Map<String, Double> scores) {
        String verdict = "allow";
        for (var e : scores.entrySet()) {
            double[] t = THRESH.getOrDefault(e.getKey(), new double[]{0.40, 0.85});
            if (e.getValue() >= t[1]) return "block";   // worst case wins immediately
            if (e.getValue() >= t[0]) verdict = "review";
        }
        return verdict;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // prints: review
        System.out.println(decide(Map.of("hate", 0.5, "spam", 0.1)));
    }
}

Failure patterns: scores are not calibrated probabilities (0.8 from one vendor is not 0.8 from another); a model update shifts the score distribution and silently moves your block rate, so track block rate per day; adversarial users probe the boundary with misspellings, other languages, leetspeak, or splitting a message across turns; over-blocking medical or educational content frustrates legitimate users.

Analogy: a smoke alarm. Too sensitive and it goes off for toast; too dull and it misses the fire. You tune it to the room.

Common interview traps.

  • Using one threshold. The middle band for review is the design.
  • Quoting accuracy. With 1% bad content, blocking nothing is 99% accurate; use precision and recall.
  • Reusing vendor default thresholds without measuring on your own traffic.
  • Same threshold for every category.

notes.title: Human review: queues, SLAs and the feedback loop
notes.html:
Human review handles the uncertain middle band and appeals. Humans are slow and costly, so treat their time as a scarce resource and design around it.

Architecture:

classifier (review band) --> priority queue --> reviewer tool --> decision
                                  ^                                  |
                                  |                                  v
                      sampled "allowed" and "blocked"     labels + audit log
                      items (for QA)                               |
                                                                   v
                                                  retrain / retune thresholds

Key design points:

  • Priority: order the queue by severity and by score and age. Self-harm or child-safety items jump the queue with a short SLA (service level agreement, a promised response time, for example 15 minutes versus 24 hours for spam).
  • Sampling for QA: also sample items the system auto-allowed and auto-blocked. Without this you never learn about false negatives (bad content that passed) because nobody looked.
  • Two reviewers for hard categories, with a third to break ties; track inter-reviewer agreement, since low agreement means your policy text is unclear, not that reviewers are bad.
  • Reviewer wellbeing: harmful content harms people. Blur images and audio by default, rotate duties, limit exposure, provide support. Voice items: show the transcript first, play audio on demand.
  • Decision actions: allow, remove, warn, rate-limit, suspend, escalate to legal or law enforcement for the most serious classes. Every decision stores the policy version, reviewer id, timestamp and evidence in an immutable audit log, which you need for appeals and regulators.
  • Appeals: let users contest; a different reviewer decides.
  • Privacy: reviewers see user data, so use role-based access, redact personal data where possible, log access.

Pending-state behaviour is a product decision. Pre-moderation holds content until reviewed (safe, slow, used for kids' content). Post-moderation publishes immediately and reviews later (fast, risky). A common compromise is to publish low-risk items and hold items in the review band, with the limited visibility of "only the author sees it" (shadow state) until a decision arrives.

A simple queue ordering in code (using a priority queue; lower number first):

import heapq, time

q = []
def enqueue(item_id, severity, score):
    # severity 1 = most urgent; higher score first; older first via time tiebreak
    heapq.heappush(q, (severity, -score, time.time(), item_id))

enqueue("a", 3, 0.55); enqueue("b", 1, 0.60); enqueue("c", 3, 0.80)
print([heapq.heappop(q)[3] for _ in range(3)])   # prints: ['b', 'c', 'a']
import java.util.PriorityQueue

data class Item(val id: String, val severity: Int, val score: Double, val ts: Long)

fun main() {
    val q = PriorityQueue(compareBy<Item>({ it.severity }, { -it.score }, { it.ts }))
    q += Item("a", 3, 0.55, 1); q += Item("b", 1, 0.60, 2); q += Item("c", 3, 0.80, 3)
    println(generateSequence { q.poll() }.map { it.id }.toList())   // prints: [b, c, a]
}
import java.util.*;

public class ReviewQueue {
    record Item(String id, int severity, double score, long ts) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PriorityQueue<Item> q = new PriorityQueue<>(
            Comparator.comparingInt(Item::severity)
                      .thenComparing(Comparator.comparingDouble(Item::score).reversed())
                      .thenComparingLong(Item::ts));
        q.add(new Item("a", 3, 0.55, 1)); q.add(new Item("b", 1, 0.60, 2)); q.add(new Item("c", 3, 0.80, 3));
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!q.isEmpty()) out.add(q.poll().id());
        System.out.println(out);   // prints: [b, c, a]
    }
}

Capacity math: if 1,000,000 items per day are scored and 0.5% land in the review band, that is 5,000 items. A reviewer handling one item per 30 seconds for 6 productive hours does 6 x 3,600 / 30 = 720 items a day, so you need about 5,000 / 720 = 7 reviewers per day before QA sampling and shifts. If a launch doubles traffic, the queue doubles; so also design a load-shedding rule (for instance narrow the band, or hold low-severity categories longer) rather than letting SLAs collapse.

Real examples: large social platforms use classifier plus human review tiers and an oversight appeals process; OpenAI, Anthropic and others describe automated classifiers plus human review for policy enforcement (verify public descriptions); marketplaces like Airbnb and Etsy run review queues for listings.

Failure patterns: the queue grows unbounded and old items rot; reviewers disagree because guidelines are vague; labels never flow back so the classifier never improves; a bug routes everything to review at 3 a.m.; audit logs missing so an appeal cannot be answered.

Analogy: a hospital emergency room. A triage nurse sorts by urgency so the doctor (scarce) sees the dangerous cases first, and later reviews outcomes to improve triage.

Common interview traps.

  • Sending everything uncertain to humans without computing capacity.
  • Only sampling blocked items, so false negatives stay invisible.
  • No SLA tiers: a self-harm report waiting a day is a serious failure.
  • Skipping reviewer protections and audit trail.

notes.title: Putting it together: a voice assistant design in five steps
notes.html:
A typical senior interview question: "Design a voice assistant in a kids' learning app that must feel instant, protect privacy and stay safe." Answer by walking the layers.

  1. Edge: on-device wake word and VAD, local echo cancellation, local TTS fallback. Why: battery, privacy, offline.
  2. Transport: WebSocket or WebRTC to your backend (never the model vendor directly with a shipped key); Opus audio; ping and reconnect.
  3. Cascade: streaming ASR -> adaptive endpointing -> LLM stream -> sentence-level TTS stream, each cancellable per turn id. Target time to first audio under about one second.
  4. Safety: input check on the transcript, output check per sentence before TTS, action gate for anything that spends money or shares data, stricter category thresholds for child users (low thresholds, high human-review rate), a "stop and hand off to a safe response" path for self-harm.
  5. Operations: log per-stage latency (p50, p95), barge-in rate, endpoint cut-off rate, block rate by category, review-queue age; sample conversations to humans; alert on drift.
phone: wake+VAD+AEC --Opus/WebSocket--> gateway --> ASR --> input moderation
                                                              |
phone: speaker <--audio chunks-- TTS <-- output moderation <-- LLM (cancellable)
                                                              |
                         async sampling --> human review --> labels --> thresholds

The key insight to state out loud: sentence-level output moderation adds delay equal to roughly one sentence of LLM generation (for example 15 tokens / 50 tok/s = 0.3 s) plus classifier time, which you pay for safety, and you can hide part of it by running the classifier concurrently with TTS synthesis of that sentence and discarding both if blocked.

Failure patterns across the whole system: p95 latency is dominated by retries on the ASR vendor; a moderation outage must fail closed for high-risk categories and fail open (with logging) for low-risk ones, a conscious decision; the model gets replaced and thresholds were tuned for the old one.

Analogy: a live TV broadcast with a seven-second delay. The delay is the price of being able to bleep something harmful before it reaches the audience.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing models but not the cancellation, buffering and failure behaviour.
  • No decision about fail-open vs fail-closed when the moderator is down.
  • Not stating a latency target and measuring p95, not just the average.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• On-device vs cloud is a per-request trade-off: device wins on TTFT when warm, privacy, offline use and per-call cost; cloud wins on model quality, long outputs and fresh data. Use a hybrid router with logged paths and fallbacks, and never trust the client for safety.
  • Latency has parts (TTFT vs throughput, cold vs warm); battery trades radio energy for compute and heat; measure on real devices.
  • Voice assistants are streaming pipelines (VAD, ASR, LLM, TTS) over WebSocket or WebRTC, or one speech-to-speech model; every stage must stream and be cancellable, and a sub-second turn is mostly won in endpointing.
  • Turn-taking uses VAD plus adaptive or semantic end-of-turn detection; barge-in needs echo cancellation, a confirmation window, cancelling upstream work, turn ids on chunks and trimming history to what was actually heard.
  • Moderation is layered: input filter, output filter (hard with streaming), action gate, async audit; keep the moderator independent of the generator.
  • Thresholds are two-sided (allow, review, block), per category and per surface, tuned on your own labelled traffic using precision and recall, and monitored for drift.
  • Human review needs priority and SLA tiers, capacity maths, QA sampling of allowed items, reviewer protection, audit logs, appeals and a feedback loop into the classifier.
  • Unverified (mark verify): specific product names and event names (Realtime API, Gemini Live, Llama Guard, Bedrock Guardrails, turn-detector models), Android permission details by API level, and all latency and cost figures, which are illustrative.
